publications.title: Proximal State Nudging: Reducing Skill Atrophy from AI Assistance
publications.subtitle: International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 2026
publications.description: Presented in person in Seoul, South KoreaSkill atrophy, the gradual decline of human capability under AI assistance, poses a safety risk in shared-control of semi-autonomous systems, where operators may be unable to distinguish their own inputs from autonomous corrections. We propose Proximal State Nudging (PSN), a shared autonomy algorithm that jointly optimizes for skill development and task performance by nudging users toward states estimated to be most learnable. We first show that PSN outperforms existing shared autonomy baselines in balancing student improvement in unassisted reward with overall shared performance, using simulated students in the classic LunarLander environment. We then present, to the best of our knowledge, the first human subject studies of a planner incorporating learning-compatible shared autonomy: across two driving tasks in the CARLA simulator (High Performance Racing and Parallel Parking, n = 60), PSN produces up to 7x larger gains in unassisted skill than standard blended shared autonomy, while incurring 50 fewer collisions than unassisted self-practice.

publications.title: Intent at a Glance: Gaze-Guided Robotic Manipulation via Foundation Models
publications.subtitle: Robotics: Science & Systems (RSS) 2025
publications.description: Presented in person in Los Angeles, CaliforniaDesigning intuitive interfaces for robotic control remains a central challenge in enabling effective human-robot interaction, particularly in assistive care settings. Eye gaze offers a fast, non-intrusive, and intent-rich input modality, making it an attractive channel for conveying user goals. In this work, we present GAMMA (Gaze Assisted Manipulation for Modular Autonomy), a system that leverages ego-centric gaze tracking and a vision-language model to infer user intent and autonomously execute robotic manipulation tasks. By contextualizing gaze fixations within the scene, the system maps visual attention to high-level semantic understanding, enabling skill selection and parameterization without task-specific training. We evaluate GAMMA on a range of table-top manipulation tasks and compare it against baseline gaze-based control without reasoning. Results demonstrate that GAMMA provides robust, intuitive, and generalizable control, highlighting the potential of combining foundation models and gaze for natural and scalable robot autonomy. publications.title: Optimization of Swim Pose Estimation and Recognition with Data Augmentation
publications.subtitle: IEEE Southwest Symposium on Image Analysis and Interpretation (SSIAI 2024)
publications.description: Presented in person at Santa Fe, New MexicoSwim pose estimation and recognition is a challenging problem in machine learning and artificial intelligence as the body of the swimmer is continuously submerged under the water. The objective of this paper is to enhance existing ML models for estimating swim poses and for recognizing strokes to aid swimmers in pursuing a more perfect technique. We developed a novel methodology augmenting raw video data and adjusting a YOLOv7 base model to enhance swim pose estimation.

publications.title: Design and Analysis of an FPGA-based CNN for Exercise Recognition
publications.subtitle: IEEE TRON Symposium (TRONSHOW 2023)
publications.description: Presented by first author Derrick Trinh (virtually) in TRON Symposium, hosted in Tokyo, JapanIn this paper, we describe the design and analysis of an FPGA-based exercise detector, and show the improvement in performance of an FPGA-based over a GPU-based human action recognition application. Using the Xilinx Kria KV260 development board and a USB webcam, the pose of a person is tracked to determine what kind of exercise they are doing. OpenPose is used to obtain the coordinates of a person’s body parts. Using Vitis AI and Tensorflow, multiple neural networks to identify different exercises were designed using a sequence of the coordinates as an input. These models have different input sizes and number of convolutional layers. These neural network models were run directly on the programmable logic (Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC FPGA) of the Kria board, and their performance in frames per second (FPS) was analyzed. Our simulation results show that the FPGA’s performance based on a relatively simple CNN reached 372 to 722 FPS while the ResNet-based GPU (Jetson Nano) performance was 32 FPS, for which the accuracy degradation is less than 10%.

activity.title: I'm at #ICML2026 🇰🇷 to present our new work on reducing skill atrophy from AI overreliance with Toyota Research Institute ! As AI systems improve their capabilities, how can we use them to also support a human user’s own skill development? At the #AI4GOOD workshop, I’ll be presenting Proximal State Nudging (PSN): an assistance algorithm that balances between task performance and human learning. https://lnkd.in/gShT9nUn We were inspired by control tasks (surgery, driving, teleoperation) where AI has been shown to improve task safety and performance, but also has a deskilling effect on people! For example: • Medicine ( https://lnkd.in/gynVuqqx ) • Driving ( https://lnkd.in/g5ddkbpa ) • Coding ( https://lnkd.in/g-pcKaVw ) Prior works often remove AI support entirely so that people can learn. PSN offers a new option: modulate *how* AI assistance is given in order to both ensure safe performance and scaffold human learning. PSN works by (i) estimating which environment states are most “learnable” for an individual user, and then (ii) adjusting the *level* and *type” of AI assistance to gradually nudge the user to these states, while still optimizing for task reward. Similar to how a parent might hold and help their kid learning how to ride a bike! 😊 We evaluate PSN in both the Lunar Lander environment and with 60 human participants in two CARLA driving tasks: parallel parking and high-performance racing. PSN produced up to 7x gains in unassisted skill learning compared to standard shared autonomy methods, while incurring 50% fewer collisions than unassisted self-practice. This is joint work with Yuchen Cui Deepak Gopinath, PhD Emily Sumner, PhD and Guy Rosman , and I’ll be at ICML if interested in learning more! ...more ...more

So....how are students expected to figure out which university recruiter is supposed to be recruiting for what? I highkey think it is running it down mid when people encourage students to reach out to recruiters, but not specify to them the person they're reaching out to might not (A) be a university recruiter in the first place, (B) be the aligned recruiter for what they're interested in, or (C) be someone that can even help. All the while, they burn their precious InMail credits in doing so. I think students are frustrated with recruiting because they don't know who is responsible for what, because they believe that knowing will give them an edge. At the same time, I am experienced enough to know that everyone has different worldviews when it comes to their social media and privacy, and a response is not owed. Which is why most recruiters might not be respond to LinkedIn messages. The thing is, if it stands that there are those who don't respond to messages, it stands to reason that some 𝐦𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭. In that vein, my reminder to my students is this - congratulation posts and announcement posts do serve a purpose, and this can help if you plan ahead. When written on LinkedIn , students usually thank their recruiting coordinators, sourcers, and/or university recruiters that they've worked with. I can happily confirm this because I'm tagged in these posts. So if that connection of yours has the internship/new grad role you're specifically interested in, they likely have survived the recruiting process and those people they've thanked, were 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐯𝐞𝐝 with their recruiting in that genre of internship. hint >_> hint >_> !!!! hint >_> !!!!!!!!!!!!! Check their profiles. Check their job title. Check their posts. Use context clues to come to a conclusion. Then, send a message respectfully. And be mindful of the calendar too! The world is a big place and recruiters are 𝐧𝐨𝐭 all the same. In the vein that some recruiters don't respond to everyone, then there has to be recruiters that sincerely try when they can. So it is my hope that this advice helps students find those rare recruiters, because I promise that they do exist! I choose to believe that there are recruiters out there that do fight the good fight and when they find windows for air, they respond where they can. Whether they are able to help depends entirely on circumstance, so please be mature enough to accept this. I do believe there are lots of kind recruiters out there, because I choose to believe there are kind people. You'd be surprised how big the world is and what kind of internships exist, when you look at different avenues that others aren't. I hope this helps :)

Just this past Tuesday night, when I finished babysitting my Codex "/goal" and went to bed, I did not expect to wake up at 3AM to a message saying that my role at the Amazon AGI SF Lab had been eliminated. It turned out that it was not just me—the entire lab had been shut down. I am still processing the news, but I have calmed down enough to reflect on my one year and two months at the lab. It was my first full-time job, and it was a team and mission that I cared about deeply. Looking back, the feeling that stands out most is gratitude. First, I want to thank my manager, Xiangjun (XJ) Wang , for allowing me to enter the world of large-scale reinforcement learning for agent training. I still remember we started on veRL, added vision-language model(VLM) support, and integrated internal WebGym environments so we could train RL exceeding 1,000 steps, and we delivered Nova Act at last year’s re:Invent, pushing the frontier of computer-use agents(CUA). This year, with only two engineers, we migrated to Slime to take advantage of its modular architecture and stronger support for asynchronous RL. We improved its fully asynchronous training, added support for long-horizon agent training, and ultimately used it to train a 100B MoE model that achieved 70 on SWE-bench Verified and 45 on Terminal-Bench, surpassing GPT-OSS, Nemotron 3 super, and Gemm4 31B. After DeepSeek V4 was released, we decided to scale our RL even further, toward models with more than 1T+ parameters. We migrated to Miles for faster support of open-source models and better compatibility with Blackwell GPUs. We were almost there. The mid-train was nearly complete. The RL data was ready. And then, everything stopped. I am equally grateful to my talented and extraordinarily reliable colleagues. You have been my closest friends, collaborators, and teachers. One of the things I valued most about this team was that there was no rigid boundary between infra and algorithms. Cross-disciplinary collaboration was not only encouraged—it was essential. Many of the hardest problems in RL require expertise from both sides. For example, truncated importance sampling(TIS) is an algo solution to a difficult systems problem: the mismatch between training and inference engines. Our fully asynchronous RL training recipe was also the result of close collaboration between infrastructure and algorithm researchers. Also, as someone who wants to understand the entire stack, I learned far more than infra alone. PPO, GRPO, value functions, etc., are no longer black boxes to me; data triage and curation were equally fascinating; I learned which metrics matter for evaluating an RL run. The list goes on. This experience will remain one of the highlights of my life. I will remember this team, the problems we tackled, and everything we built together. I wish everyone the very best, and I sincerely hope our paths cross again. Finally, I am open to new opportunities. #OpenToWork
